Hi, everybody,

I just got back home from GenCon about 2 hours ago and am
trying to hold onto consciousness after two nights of V:TES
passed the 4 o'clock hour in the A.M.

Thursday, Joe Churchill judged the tournament, so I'll leave
it to him to comment on that day. Rumor has it that a deck
constructed under 4CL that focused around intercept won?!

On Friday, we had a draft tournament, originally supposed to
be Rochester. Scott Larabee, bless his soul, took our advise
to let us run our own draft format. Among those in attendance,
we went with a Michigan draft. About 25 players participated.
I'm thinking Dave Tatu won, but my sleepiness is telling me
Jared Strait might have won....and my notes are at home not
with me here at work where I had to come fix some things.....
Better, stop there.... Galen Cruze had a VP with a 3
players with 0. The winner got about half a box worth of
AH, DS, and Sabbat. The others got significant numbers as
well.

Friday night, we played some informal after consuming alcoholic
beverages with Robert Goudie, Dave Tatu, Keith Thompson, Joe
Churchill, Mike Courtouis, and myself in attendance. In the
last game, I was quickly ousted at 4 a.m. and allowed to go
get some sleep to judge on Saturday.

Saturday was the Championship event with Jarett Welch capturing
the title after eeking into the final round with only 5 VP's.
Dave Tatu was in with 9, Robert Goudie with 10, Keith Thompson
with 6.5, and Greg Ciallella with 7 were the other finalists.
There were 22 people to start the event with
Jarret's deck was Presence bleed with some votes, and he will
hopefully be e-mailing his deck to me soon for posting and for
inclusion in the Fragment. Every player also got Championship Event
t-shirts with some Necromancy card that I can't remember either
on them (Compel the Spirit?) Jarett received a goblet consisting
of a porcelain skull mounted on a pewter base valued at over
$150 plus a king's ransom in AH, DS, and Sabbat.

Saturday night, Scott Larabee and Dave Whose-last-name-I-can't-
remember were kind enough to give us the remaining sealed V:TES
starters and boosters for an informal draft tournament later
that night with 8 participants. When the second round was
completed at 5 a.m. most of us left in exhaustion and split of
the rest of the cards. Robert Goudie, Dave Tatu, Joe Churchill,
Jesse whose-last-name-I-can't-remember-but-it-was-German, Galen
Cruze, Keith Thompson, Mike Courtouis, and myself participated.

Sunday morning, I awoke in a panic at about 10 thinking it was
the middle of the afternoon and leapt into the shower only to
come out and realise it was only 9:30 a.m. When I arrived at
the convention, no one was to be found and after playing a
couple demos (Mechwarrior 3 computer game, Battletech miniatures,
Babylon 5 Space Combat Simulator) and getting a steal on some
Star Wars RPG books, I decided it was a hopeless cause and headed
home at 3:30 in the afternoon.

Overall, thinks went very smoothly. Everyone had fun (I hope),
and no one walked away empty handed from any event. Next year,
WotC wants V:EKN to be more involved in planning events to run
and give us a fixed play area. And no, no new news on the new
cards. How many times can you say "new/knew" in a sentence?

Uhhhh, after I get some sleep and compile all my notes, I'll
post some more substantial information.

Mike

I wonder why a number of players would like the "Michigan *Sealed with
some trade*" to be the official alternative DCI format. :)
(No offense meant Dave, just want to make clear what type it really is!)

>
> It worked just fine. We did the draft, two rounds, and a final
> in about 7 hours, IIRC. What will be interesting if we adopt
> a draft as the standard sealed-based format is to see how the
> draft develops into bargaining and such. "We seem to be going
> after the same cards. Maybe one of us should change ideas?"
> sort of things.

I really don't like the idea of trading in order to get a somewhat
competitive deck. This really *asks* for collusion between players.
Imagine two players, one trading needed cards to another under the
condition that if they sit together on a table, the one getting the
needed cards will support him or even oust himself so that the one
offering the needed cards will get at least 1 VP. Do you really think
that's cool???? I do certainly not.

I think the MD is just a basic Sealed with some limited trading at the
end to improve the deck a bit. There is no "drafting" as such.

A real draft, where you get at least some control over the cards you
get, is strongly preferable. There it is your own skill that decides
how good your deck is, with a *little* luck strewn in admittedly. In a
tournament first depending on luck for some playable cards, then
depending on "friendly" opponents to trade you some usable cards is...
crap (for a tournament, not in any other environment).
The time factor comes into play, too. First opening boosters,
constructing deck takes time. Next you waste time choosing the cards to
trade, then the trade itself costs time. Again you need time to
reconstruct the deck. Will we skip one of the preliminary rounds to
keep up a reasonable timetable? ;)

Next: Rochester Draft and similar. ehehehehe
Time consuming, and excessive. Mike said something of 1.5 to 2 hours
for 228 cards! Let's face it: when each player takes the card/s he
needs one at a time, valuable minutes are wasted. Also, the other
players actually *see* what he goes for, and can immediatly either
build a counter deck or screw him!
The best solution is the "rotary principle", where each player looks
through a number of cards without having the other seeing what he
takes; at the same time the drafting process is sped up because each
player is doing exactly the same! One card chosen, rest to the player
on the left, taking the cards from the player to the right, choosing
again, and so on. This really works, and leads to good and playable
decks without having everybody discarding like mad in the games. :)

A time limit is really necessary, otherwise the drafting process really
gets bogged down.

One final word: I really doubt that the DCI would adopt a format where
players can trade before the rounds start. This would open "a whole can
of worms" as some of you have put it in the past. I also doubt that the
DCI would like to adopt a format that is too luck-based like the simple
Sealed. Most likely they would accept a format similar to the rochester
draft, or something new altogether (like the "rotary principle" - Elder
Draft!).

The format we propose should be
1) not too luck-dependant
2) not too time-consuming
3) able to come up with well-playable decks
4) able to prohibit collusion prior to the rounds

MD fails to do 1) 2) 3) and 4), Rochester fails in clearly in 2) and
maybe even in the other points as well (don't know right now).
The Elder Draft OTOH would be (almost) invulnerable to the above points.

I understand that almost nobody has experience with the Elder Draft,
except a few players from mid-Europe. I also understand that a version
of the Rochester was played at GenCon and made rather good progress.
And finally I understand all the players familiar with the MD
(naturally the MJL now NJL players :) ) who did invest a lot of time
and effort in inventing a good solid Sealed format.

Carl

Actually, you take 1 vampire at a time and 2 library cards at a
time. And that was way more cords than you should do, which I
stated. The actual tournament had a starter and a booster: 94
cards (or is it 93 or 95?). Most of the tables were done in
1 to 1.5 hours. A couple took longer.

> Also, the other players actually *see* what he goes for, and can
> immediatly either build a counter deck or screw him!

So? They've basically set themselves up to lose if all they
draft is an anti-deck for one of the others at the table. Second,
if you have a large group, they may never play each other as players
are reseated after the draft. Plus, once you start going for
things, you have to consider the cards that are coming up that
could hose your deck. For example on Saturday night, I was going
for permanent rush (Havens, Wynn, Roxanne, Ebaneezer) and guns
as part of my strategy. So I grabbed Illegal Search and Seizure
and Peace Treaty whenever there wasn't other stuff available that
I absolutely wanted.

> The best solution is the "rotary principle",

I really don't think there's a problem, so no solution is
necessary. :)

> A time limit is really necessary, otherwise the drafting process
> really gets bogged down.

Having a fixed limit would be bad. What could be done is handing
out warnings for taking a long time for picking cards. Another
player at the table brings it to the judge's attention, and he
can then view the draft for a couple minutes to see how it goes.
If a player is slow, he can give an unrecorded warning to speed
up and issue a tracked warning if he is called to the table again.

> The format we propose should be
> 1) not too luck-dependant
> 2) not too time-consuming
> 3) able to come up with well-playable decks
> 4) able to prohibit collusion prior to the rounds
>
> MD fails to do 1) 2) 3) and 4), Rochester fails in clearly in 2) and
> maybe even in the other points as well (don't know right now).
> The Elder Draft OTOH would be (almost) invulnerable to the above
> points.

I don't think a Rochester-based draft is really that slow.
The judge just needs to be prepared to give warnings for taking
a long time to choose.

I think the Elder Draft would be more susceptible to cheating.
People who are capable can easily take 3 cards when they should
only take 2. So if you then count their decks, you have to redo
the draft and decide whether the player did it on purpose. This
is impossible under the "GenCon" draft unless no one at the
table is paying attention in which case those players deserve to
be screwed.

I think the Elder Draft would also take longer than regular draft
because all the players don't see the cards at once. That means
each has to take time to view the cards in the booster and decide
what he wants. Player 4 can't start thinking about what he wants
until the booster gets around to him.

> I understand that almost nobody has experience with the Elder Draft,
> except a few players from mid-Europe. I also understand that a
> version of the Rochester was played at GenCon and made rather good
> progress. And finally I understand all the players familiar with
> the MD (naturally the MJL now NJL players :) ) who did invest a lot
> of time and effort in inventing a good solid Sealed format.

Like above, now that I've actually read all the stuff on MD, I
feel that it is too luck based. Fifteen cards is going to make
zero difference with a mostly sealed deck.

Greetings,

I have been watching the Draft format debate with interest; I
would like to see the DCI sanction both a draft and sealed deck
format.
I feel that I can add to the discussion of differences between
elder (rotary) draft and GenCon (Rochester) draft because I have
played both formats. A league here in Denver ran two draft
tournaments last year, and prior to the tournaments we tested
different draft formats.
I won’t go into great detail about the different draft
mechanics we tested, but I should mention that we used either 6
Jyhad boosters (114 cards?) or 4 Sabbat boosters (112 cards?).
Drafters build decks with at least 60 cards and 12 vamps; this
allows for a fairly focused deck if you draft well. Other things we
apparently did differently involved the drafting of vampires; we
would do a number of rounds (say 4) of library card drafts, then 1
round of vampire drafts and repeat. We also would switch draft
directions every so often so that you weren’t always drafting behind
the same person.

The major disagreements about the two draft formats appear
to be: 1) length of time for the draft, and 2) desirability of knowing
what your opponents are drafting.
1) Length of time for the draft. When drafting, we never used
time limits, because we were just testing formats. During our
testing elder draft would take approximately 45 minutes, while
GenCon draft would take approximately 60 minutes. Drafting and
deck building were generally accomplished in about 75 minutes for
both formats. Elder draft is definitely faster, however, not TWICE
as fast as GenCon draft. GenCon draft is more complicated to run,
and there is a steeper learning curve for new drafters, which
contributed some time to the length of our GenCon drafts.
2) Desirability of knowing what your opponents are drafting.
Obviously you have greater knowledge of what some of your
opponents are going to be using in GenCon draft. Whether this is
desirable or not is a matter of opinion. It is not “scouting” because
it is part of the deck building format; remember that GenCon draft is
derived from the DCI sanctioned Rochester Draft for Magic:tG.
As previously stated, GenCon draft increases the social aspect
of the game, I consider this A Good Thing. From our experiences,
counter-drafting (drafting cards that your opponent can use) occurs
in both formats, but can be used to better effect in GenCon draft; in
GenCon draft, I can target other drafters I know to be doing well,
rather than just “shooting in the dark”. Also, GenCon draft differs
more from constructed deck format than does elder draft; this is
nice if you are looking for a change of pace from constructed deck.

I personally enjoy GenCon draft much more than elder draft,
the interaction and excitement of the open draft process contributes
greatly to the overall tournament. I think that the increased
interaction of the GenCon draft more than offsets the increase in
draft time.
I’ve never seen anyone say that there is only going to be one
additional format, however.

There are fewer cards of the "mainstay cards" for these c.d.s.': I.G,
Bum's Rush, KRC, Majesty, etc. It's the overall selection that counts
in a draft. You have a *basic* strategy in mind and draft cards for it.
You will have to include a lot of otherwise "useless" cards (equipment,
votes, no-skill cards,...), that's the nature of a draft environment

purely I.G rush). Bianca with a Bastard Sword striking with a Lucky
Blow is a nice thing to behold, and awfully frightening in a Draft
environment. Same goes for votes: everyone will include vote-cards in
his deck, stupid if he didn't. 1 vote *makes* a difference, especially
with table talk.
Bleed? Yes there are good dom/pre bleed decks, but they tend not to be
weenie hordes or killing machines. Computer Hacking and Laptops are

Surprise Infulence and Delying Tactics are also often seen. Gameplay
during a Draft is not as fast-paced as in a constructed. It's more
likely that you will get unexpected help from your prey or predetor
during votes. (Experienced very often.)

A Draft is a Draft is a Draft. :) There are no well-focused decks.
Players have to work with what they get, and in the case of
dom/pre/aus/obf more than 1 clan share them, so they will most likely
be split up between players. Players going heavily for bleed will
notice that there aren't that much cards for them to use available. :)

But that's what players like about Draft: it's different.
